      Alarm Triage — think DOPE

      SCORE 0 · – / 6

      Professional method: Patient first → Displacement → Obstruction → Pneumothorax → Equipment. If you cannot explain distress in seconds: disconnect & bag on 100% O₂. 6 alarms per run, dealt unseen-first from a 12-alarm deck — at Fresh Tier 2+, generated variants with new patient contexts and pressure / saturation numbers join the run. 22 sec each.

      Most likely cause — and first safe action?

      ABG — the 3-question method

      SCORE 0 · STREAK 0

      Read every gas the same way: 1) pH acid or alkaline? 2) PaCO₂ opposite pH → respiratory. 3) HCO₃⁻ with pH → metabolic. Then: is the other value compensating? 8 gases, 18 sec each — every value is generated fresh each run so no gas ever repeats, types never repeat inside a run, and at Fresh Tier 3 compensated & mixed disorders join the pool.

      TAKE IT TO THE FLOOR

      Real-day toolkit — use this on your next clinical

      The game is rehearsal. These are the scripts to actually run with patients, preceptors, and charts.

      The 15-minute pre-round (before 07:00)

      • 1Assignment & precautions: rooms, isolation, fall/aspiration risks, code status.
      • 2Each patient: diagnosis & why they need RT today.
      • 3Latest ABG + SpO₂ trend — direction, not just the last value.
      • 4Imaging: latest chest X-ray report in one sentence.
      • 5Current therapy: device, FiO₂/flow or vent mode + key settings, PEEP.
      • 6Goal today: wean? SBT? mobilise? Write it down.

      The 60-second bedside assessment (every room)

      • 1Look: colour, WOB, chest rise, tube position / cm mark.
      • 2Monitor: SpO₂, HR, EtCO₂ — validate probe & waveform first.
      • 3Listen: breath sounds, all fields, left vs right.
      • 4Ask: “How is your breathing vs an hour ago?” Pain? Secretions?
      • 5Decide: treat, escalate (SBAR), or monitor — then reassess & chart the response.

      SBAR — say it exactly like this

      S: “Room 402, SpO₂ 88% on room air, WOB up in 20 minutes.”
      B: “Admitted yesterday with pneumonia, was 94% on 2 L this morning.”
      A: “Breath sounds diminished on the right, RR 28. I think he’s deteriorating.”
      R: “I recommend starting low-flow O₂ now and you evaluating at the bedside — can you come now?”

      Numbers in S & A, one clear ask in R. Never freelance outside your scope while you wait.

      Pocket kit — never round empty-handed

      • ✓Stethoscope (yours, on your neck)
      • ✓Bandage scissors + tape
      • ✓Notepad & pen — settings, times, questions
      • ✓Pocket guide & calculator — alveolar gas eq., cylinder duration
      • ✓Watch with seconds — RR is counted, not guessed

      How preceptors grade you — the rubric behind this game

      DomainDevelopingCompetent (pass)Proficient (hire this intern)
      Safety & AssessmentTreats before assessing; misses tube migrationAssesses first; bags when in doubtAnticipates deterioration before the alarm
      TechnicalNeeds parts handed over; settings unexplainedBuilds & calibrates independently; explains whyTroubleshoots in DOPE order under pressure
      CommunicationVague updates, no numbers, no askComplete SBAR with recommendationAsks “why this mode?”; closes the loop
      Documentation“Treatment given.” Late, from memoryPre/post vitals, tolerance & response, on timeNote shows reasoning a provider can act on
      ProfessionalismHides between tasks; defensiveEarly, visible, volunteers, accepts correctionTeam seeks them out; sites recruit them
      POCKET SKILL

      O₂ cylinder duration calculator

      Duration = (gauge − 200 psi residual) × factor ÷ flow. E = 0.28 · H/K = 3.14 · D = 0.16 · M = 1.56 · G = 2.41. Never plan on the residual.

      Check: E at 2,000 psi, 4 L/min → (2,000−200)×0.28÷4 = 126 min.
